copy.14: Abolish the political party system. Return power to all the people.
copy.15:
Fairness, impartiality, and openness: establish channels for dialogue across positions and break through information bubbles.
Pursue facts and truth with conviction: judge right and wrong, not political allegiance. Reject the substitution of emotion or moral pressure for evidence and judgments of responsibility.
copy.16: Real-time voting: continually confirm authorization and promptly replace those unfit for office.
copy.17: Reject the Grip of Party Interests
copy.18: End the binding of public office and political judgment to political parties, so that individual competence, specific proposals, and responsibility can be assessed independently.
copy.19: Prevent the Distortion of Democratic Authorization
copy.20: All public power must remain subject to public oversight. Election results must never justify rejecting accountability, obstructing the revocation of authority, or monopolizing governance.
copy.21: Beyond the Three Principles of the People
copy.22: Carry forward Sun Yat-sen’s political ideals, using modern technology to further realize the principles of government “of the people, by the people, for the people” through continuing authorization and effective accountability.
copy.23:
Bad people may speak the truth; good people may make mistakes.
Supporting Universal Popular Sovereignty does not mean endorsing all of my personal positions. Think independently, distinguish right from wrong, and follow sound ideas.
copy.45:
Argue openly; accept scrutiny.
Match power with responsibility; maintain accountability.
copy.46: Volume I / Popular Sovereignty and Public Authorization
copy.47: Public Power Comes from the People’s Continuing Authorization
copy.49: All offices are filled through examinations and public voting. Support is updated in real time: those who meet the requirements take office; those who do not leave office.
copy.50: After an election, the people should retain the practical ability to supervise, veto, and withdraw authorization.
copy.51: Universal Popular Sovereignty (UPS) regards <mark class="key-point">the people as a whole as the ultimate source of public political power</mark>. It proposes that qualified candidates for major public offices—including the highest leadership, legislators, and heads of the branches of government—be elected by the people. Authority should not arise from party allocation or mutual appointments among leaders.
copy.52: Officeholders must pass the relevant competence assessments and continuously satisfy the conditions of public support required for authorization. <mark class="key-point">Once the formal conditions for revocation of authority are met</mark>, their powers end under the system. They cannot invoke their term, position, or organizational ties to retain power.
copy.54:
Real-time authorization allows people to continually update their support or opposition.
Revocation of authority must follow previously published thresholds, necessary observation periods, buffers, and confirmation procedures. Ordinary fluctuations in support must be clearly distinguished from a formal revocation of authority.
copy.55: The Public System and Personal Positions
copy.56: UPS addresses the source and authorization of public power, and the revocation of that authority. Personal thought concerns specific value judgments and policy ideas. Supporting the former does not require accepting the latter. Any personal proposal seeking to become public policy must undergo the appropriate public discussion, expert review, and public decision-making procedures.
copy.58: The Holder of Sovereignty, Continuing Authorization, and Effective Revocation of Authority
copy.60: Everyone is an employee, including the president. The difference is that the president’s employer is the entire citizenry.
copy.62: The people may “delegate governance,” but must not be reduced to “the governed.”
copy.63: Public governance may be entrusted to competent personnel and professional institutions, but what these agents receive is conditional authority. Political status, professional qualifications, and administrative position do not make an agent a new source of sovereignty.
copy.66: The people may continually confirm, adjust, or withdraw political authorization. Participation should not be effective only during fixed election periods, and officeholders must not be able to close off oversight or mechanisms for revocation of authority themselves.
copy.69: The legitimacy of long-term officeholding depends on continuing, valid public support and <mark class="key-point">a practically exercisable right to replace the officeholder</mark>. No single vote can confer an irrevocable entitlement to permanent office.
copy.71: The People Retain the Right to Decide Their System
copy.72: The people may amend, redesign, or replace UPS through lawful procedures. The system itself remains bound by popular sovereignty and must not cancel the people’s ultimate right to decide in the name of preserving itself.
copy.74: Delegating governance does not permanently transfer sovereignty; continued officeholding does not waive the right of replacement. The confirmation and withdrawal of authorization must have verifiable, enforceable institutional channels.
copy.75: The Right to Choose a System and the Conditions of Transition
copy.76: Replacing a system requires lawful decision-making procedures, with its effects and risks fully disclosed before a decision is made. A lawful public choice of system has a different basis of legitimacy from incumbents blocking authorization channels to preserve their own position.
copy.77: Rights after a transition depend on the new system’s actual arrangements. No institutional transition should substitute unverified promises for scrutiny of the power structure and conditions for exit.
copy.79: Does a leader’s long tenure necessarily violate popular sovereignty?
copy.80: Scenario A leader receives valid support for many consecutive years. Another has served for only one year but has already blocked all routes to replacement. How should the two be judged?
copy.81: Answer The central questions are whether authorization remains valid and whether people can actually revoke the officeholder’s authority. The first leader does not automatically lose legitimacy through length of service; the second has already violated continuing authorization despite a short tenure. Term length cannot replace scrutiny of the source of power, oversight, and mechanisms for replacement.
copy.82: Must a leader be removed immediately when support briefly falls?
copy.83: Scenario An unverified video sparks controversy, and support plunges within a day. Two days later, the full footage reveals that the original clip had been selectively edited.
copy.84: Answer The system presupposes voters who remain rational, continue observing, and judge independently, rather than deciding solely on rumors. Real-time support is an oversight signal, not a formal revocation of authority. Termination depends on previously published thresholds, observation periods, buffers, and confirmation procedures. Once the formal conditions are met, an officeholder cannot remain in power by citing an unexpired term. Specific durations and figures must be established through institutional procedures, not inferred from a single example.
copy.85: Can the people choose to stop using UPS?
copy.86: Scenario Following public discussion and a lawful vote, the people decide to adopt another system, which no longer provides the same continuing means of revoking authority.
copy.87: Answer The people retain the ultimate right to amend and replace their system. UPS is fundamentally about people deciding their future together; it does not prohibit this choice to preserve itself. However, the new system’s power structure and exit conditions must be disclosed beforehand. Whether the original rights can be restored afterward depends on the new arrangements; an ongoing ability to revoke authority cannot be guaranteed. This differs from rulers unilaterally blocking people’s rights without authorization.
copy.89: Admitting a mistake is no disgrace; correcting it promptly is the right response.
copy.91: Public Participation, Competence Requirements, and the Division of Governance
copy.93: Voting eligibility must be earned through an examination, not determined solely by age. Those proposing a decision must explain it clearly to the public; if they do not, opponents may question them point by point.
copy.94: Public policies, laws, budgets, and their important reasons and details should, in principle, be open to everyone. People have opportunities to participate, vote, and scrutinize. Experts research and explain; administrative bodies implement; representatives coordinate. This division of roles does not change the fact that public power ultimately rests with the people.
copy.96: Routes to participation eligibility should be equally open. Basic examinations assess comprehension, evidence, and reasoning, <mark class="key-point">without screening for political positions</mark>. Those meeting the basic requirements retain basic participation rights. People may choose to participate, express no opinion, or abstain on each issue, while sharing the outcomes of public decisions.
copy.98: The highest leadership may consist of one person, several people, or no such office. Its purpose is to integrate policy, coordinate administration, and bear responsibility. Professional qualifications and issue-specific weighting may be designed under the rules, but must not become irrevocable public sovereignty above the people.
copy.99: An Integrated National Application and Safeguards for Participation
copy.100: The integrated national application is essential infrastructure bringing together political participation, legal information, public services, policy discussion, voting, and authorization records. Identity verification, fact-checking, reporting channels, and protection against retaliation should jointly enable people to exercise their rights in practice.
copy.101: The platform’s specific technology may be replaced, but its security, verifiability, and participation functions must be maintained. Formal voting requires sufficient information, public debate, and reasonable time limits. Continuously measured support must not independently replace formal decisions reached through lawful procedures.
copy.103: How can people participate in public decisions without possessing every kind of expertise?
copy.104: Scenario Procuring medical equipment involves technical specifications. Ordinary citizens cannot personally verify every performance claim, but still need to judge whether the expenditure is reasonable and alternatives have been adequately considered.
copy.105: Answer Public participation does not require everyone to be an expert in everything. Experts should disclose data, risks, and the basis of comparisons, and accept scrutiny across positions. People may participate, express no opinion, or abstain according to their understanding. Eligibility assessments should test comprehension and reasoning, not require support for a particular policy to pass. Professional specialization does not give experts irrevocable sovereignty.
copy.106: If every proposal has obvious flaws, must one still be selected?
copy.107: Scenario Three transport plans respectively lack a financial assessment, ignore relocation impacts, or omit verifiable demand data. Citizens consider all three inadequate for a decision.
copy.108: Answer Participation should not be confined to choosing reluctantly among inadequate options. Procedures should allow people to express no opinion, or reject all proposals and request new ones. Resubmission must address the reasons for rejection and meet waiting-period or resubmission requirements. Renaming a proposal must not permit repeated attempts to force acceptance of the same content.
copy.109: Is the integrated national application the system itself?
copy.110: Scenario The original application’s technology becomes outdated. A new platform can provide identity verification, public verification, and voting records more reliably.
copy.111: Answer The application is essential infrastructure for political participation and public services. Its name, interface, and particular technology are not irreplaceable. Tools may be updated, but security, verifiability, and practical participation must remain intact. Real-time support displayed in an interface cannot replace formal decision-making with sufficient information, public debate, and reasonable time limits.
copy.113: Integrates supporting functions including personal information, banking, the latest policies, legal consultation, police reporting, and spending.
copy.116: Open Evidence, Debate Across Positions, and Rational Judgment
copy.118: Everyone must face open questioning. Staying in a comfort zone and talking past one another is simply a waste of time.
copy.120: Communication means persuading yourself and persuading others;<br class="desktop-break">it also means allowing others to persuade you.
copy.121: The government should establish a public forum for adversarial examination, allowing supporters, opponents, and the undecided to present evidence, face follow-up questions, and answer challenges. Discussions within groups must connect to scrutiny across positions, preventing closed communities from repeatedly reinforcing existing beliefs. Judgments should rest on the evidence and reasoning of a statement itself, rather than being predetermined by its speaker’s identity, camp, or moral reputation.
copy.122: Disclose the full basis: publish original data, analytical models, limitations, and relevant interests so the reasoning process can be checked.
copy.123: Protect rebuttal and correction: provide mechanisms to label, respond to, verify, and correct false information, selectively edited clips, and misleading presentations.
copy.124: Distinguish uncertainty from established conclusions: an inability to refute a claim immediately does not prove it; an unresolved question should not be presented as a definitive answer.
copy.126: <mark class="key-point">Majority support constitutes political authorization, not proof of factual truth.</mark> Even a widely accepted claim must remain open to examination against evidence. Where evidence is insufficient, judgment should honestly be reserved.
copy.128: Does overwhelming public support prove that a policy’s factual basis is correct?
copy.129: Scenario Ninety percent of participants support building a bridge, but a subsequent independent inspection finds that the load-bearing model omitted a critical condition.
copy.130: Answer The level of support may confer political authorization, but cannot make an incorrect engineering model correct. New evidence must still undergo public verification, with remedies, suspension, or review under the rules where necessary. Ninety percent is only this example’s assumption, not a preset approval threshold. Factual judgments and authorization judgments must be treated separately.
copy.131: If an allegation cannot be refuted immediately, must it be accepted as true?
copy.132: Scenario Someone accuses a contractor of falsifying a report but supplies no original files. The contractor has not yet completed a response.
copy.133: Answer Failure to respond immediately does not prove the allegation, and lack of evidence does not prove the opposite proposition. Original data, revision records, and relevant interests should be examined, with opportunities for all parties to respond. The accuser’s camp, reputation, or past evaluations cannot replace evidence in this case. Where information is insufficient, judgment should be reserved.
copy.135: Responsibility for Decisions, Policy Stability, and Review Mechanisms
copy.137: Every policy carries duties to explain clearly, correct promptly, and share the consequences.
copy.138: Public decisions should disclose expected benefits, risks, and transition costs beforehand, and be assessed afterward against records and actual results. <mark class="key-point">Supporters, opponents, and abstainers generally share the public consequences.</mark> Errors of judgment must be distinguished from unlawful conduct; those who conceal, fabricate, or deliberately mislead bear separate personal responsibility.
copy.139: Proposal and Public ReasoningDisclose policy aims, risks, expected transitional hardship, and alternatives.
copy.140: Decision and Allocation of ResponsibilitySpecify implementation powers and duties, observation periods, and assessment criteria.
copy.141: Implementation and Verification of ResultsKeep complete records and examine outcomes, deviations, and causation.
copy.142: Remedies and Renewed Decision-MakingInitiate remedies, suspension, revision, or termination when the conditions are met.
copy.144: Policies should establish minimum observation periods and assessment indicators in advance. Without serious harm, short-term discomfort should not directly overturn a decision. Rejected proposals may be resubmitted only after the required waiting period or with new grounds sufficient to address the original reasons for rejection.
copy.146: Significant new evidence, warning signs, or harm substantially exceeding expectations may trigger early review under the rules. The more irreversible a decision—such as death, war, or irreparable destruction—the higher its advance approval threshold and scrutiny requirements should be.
copy.147: How to Address Results That Depart from Expectations
copy.148: When policy outcomes diverge substantially from expectations, first determine the causes, propose remedies, and assess whether the published review conditions are met. An observation period cannot justify refusing to address serious harm; one adverse indicator does not automatically prove that the entire policy has failed.
copy.149: Time-limited subsidies and emergency measures should include conditions for termination or renewed authorization. Long-term construction may be reviewed for sufficient reasons. Assessment should focus on remaining costs, completion levels, and future benefits, avoiding the use of past investment to bind future decisions.
copy.151: Can a policy be adjusted during its observation period if serious harm occurs?
copy.152: Scenario A policy was expected to raise short-term unemployment by one percentage point. After implementation, unemployment rises by eight percentage points, with data suggesting further deterioration.
copy.153: Answer Observation periods prevent expected short-term hardship from being mistaken for failure; they do not justify refusing to address serious harm. First examine the effects of the policy, external factors, and statistical changes, then initiate remedies or early review under the published conditions. Implementation may be suspended if necessary. The figures here illustrate a substantial deviation and do not establish a fixed review threshold.
copy.154: Can a rejected proposal be put to another vote simply by renaming it?
copy.155: Scenario A construction project is rejected over safety concerns. Its proposer resubmits it under another name the next day. In a different case, new independent testing adequately addresses the original concerns.
copy.156: Answer A change of name provides no new substantive grounds and cannot bypass the waiting period. Where new evidence genuinely addresses the reasons for rejection, an application for resubmission or a waiver of the wait may be made under the rules. Public scrutiny is still required; the proposer cannot simply declare the issue resolved. Once implementation has begun, review conditions must also account for necessary decision stability.
copy.157: Must a project continue once it is ninety percent complete?
copy.158: Scenario Most of a facility’s budget has already been spent, but the latest assessment shows a sharp decline in demand. Completion would also entail long-term maintenance costs.
copy.159: Answer Costs already incurred cannot alone determine further investment. Compare remaining construction and maintenance costs, future benefits, and the consequences of stopping, repurposing, or completing the project. Completion level is assessment data, not a command to continue. Equally, a past policy error does not justify ignoring benefits that completion may still deliver.
copy.160: Minorities · The Body · Limits on Power
copy.161: Majority Decisions, Those Directly Affected, and the Limits of Power
copy.163: There is no place for a majority decision that violently takes a person’s life; nor are property holdouts allowed to undermine the public interest.
copy.164: Public decisions should address both overall interests and <mark class="key-point">the rights of those directly affected</mark>. When relocation or losses borne by a specific group are involved, that group’s participation in the decision, review procedures, and compensation arrangements must be protected. An outside majority’s numerical advantage alone cannot justify their sacrifice.
copy.165: Majority rule must not replace an individual’s autonomous consent concerning their life and body.
copy.166: Collective decisions and compensation concerning property may be discussed under adequate procedures. Autonomy over life and the body cannot simply follow the same logic. The public interest does not authorize arbitrary deprivation of an innocent person’s life.
copy.167: For extreme decisions potentially driven by incitement or strong emotion, a leader may lawfully invoke a one-time reconsideration and cooling-off mechanism. Once the decision passes lawfully again, it must be implemented. Reconsideration must not become a tool for permanently rejecting the people’s decisions.
copy.168: Authorization and Termination of Emergency Powers
copy.169: Emergency powers require clear conditions for activation, application, and termination. Normal arrangements should resume when the crisis ends. An emergency must not permanently cut off public oversight, renewed authorization, or revocation of authority.
copy.170: The system should recognize that anyone may abuse power and therefore establish records, oversight, reporting channels, and verification mechanisms. Risk prevention must still be distinguished from individual conviction: possibility alone does not prove a specific crime.
copy.172: Does benefit to the majority justify requiring a minority to relocate or sacrifice their bodies?
copy.173: Scenario Widening a road requires some residents to relocate. Another proposal would sacrifice an innocent person to obtain organs to save several others.
copy.174: Answer The two cases cannot follow the same compensation logic. Property decisions must address the directly affected group’s participation, applicable thresholds, review, and compensation; an outside majority alone is insufficient. Autonomous consent concerning life and the body cannot be replaced by a majority vote. Saving more people does not authorize the arbitrary sacrifice of an innocent person.
copy.175: May a leader keep refusing to implement a decision they consider irrational?
copy.176: Scenario A controversial decision passes amid heightened emotions. The leader identifies specific risks and lawfully initiates reconsideration and a cooling-off period. The people then lawfully approve the same decision again.
copy.177: Answer A leader may invoke reconsideration once, allowing the reasons and risks to be examined again. Once the decision passes lawfully again, it must be implemented. The leader cannot repeatedly prolong a veto by claiming the people still do not understand, nor turn personal expertise into permanent decision-making power above the people.
copy.178: Can an emergency justify concentrating power over the long term?
copy.179: Scenario During a major disaster, an administrative body receives temporary resource-allocation powers. After the disaster ends, it refuses to relinquish them, citing the possibility of another disaster in the future.
copy.180: Answer Emergency powers require clear conditions for activation, application, and termination, with records, oversight, and verification retained. Normal arrangements should resume after the crisis. Abstract future risks cannot indefinitely prolong exceptional powers. Preventing abuse also does not mean presuming someone guilty; individual responsibility must be determined from specific conduct and evidence.
copy.182: Institutional Scrutiny, Implementation Conditions, and Practical Limits
copy.184: Everyone decides the rules together; the rules are then carried out automatically, like clockwork.
copy.185: The people jointly decide the rules, powers are exercised under specified conditions, and the system itself remains open to scrutiny.
copy.186: In re-examining the system, I identified the following issues needing further explanation. AI helped raise objections and check inferences, but its judgments do not thereby become settled conclusions. This section supplements the conditions for implementation and practical limits. Unsettled approaches still require public discussion and appropriate procedures; identifying a problem must not be presented as having completed its solution.
copy.188: The specific rules of UPS should be <mark class="key-point">jointly formulated, reviewed, and revised by the people as a whole</mark>. The system’s proposer may offer a framework, explain its reasoning, and respond to challenges, but gains no special power to decide the rules for everyone merely by having proposed it first.
copy.189: Qualification standards, authorization thresholds, the scope of powers, and conditions for revocation of authority must all undergo public discussion and appropriate decision-making procedures. The ideas presented here do not become binding rules for everyone simply because I proposed them.
copy.190: II. How Are Powers Actually Granted and Revoked?
copy.191: Public powers should be acquired, restricted, and terminated through a computer system applying rules established by the people. When qualifications, valid support, and necessary procedures satisfy the conditions for office, the system grants the corresponding powers. When conditions for restriction or revocation of authority are formally met, the system adjusts or revokes permissions under the rules.
copy.192: This principle applies equally to the president, judges, and other public offices, although their specific conditions may differ. Officeholders cannot decide for themselves whether to accept applicable restrictions, nor make a valid revocation of authority contingent on their consent.
copy.193: Automatic implementation does not eliminate observation periods, confirmation procedures, or lawful remedies. It translates established rules and formal outcomes into changes of authority. The system’s ability to execute rules does not give it the power to create political rules on its own.
copy.194: III. What If Rules Are Unclear or Facts Are Disputed?
copy.195: Automatic implementation requires clear conditions of application. The accuracy of qualification records, credibility of evidence, and completion of procedures may remain disputed. Entering information into a system does not prove that it is true.
copy.196: Which matters can be checked directly, which require fact-checking, interpretation, or review, and how powers should be handled during disputes are institutional questions that still need explicit rules. This section does not assume that computers can resolve every dispute themselves, nor present procedures not yet established as settled answers.
copy.197: IV. Does Revoking System Permissions Resolve the Real-World Problem?
copy.198: The invalidation of electronic permissions, the physical handover of duties and resources, and the handling of noncompliance are distinct issues. A system can stop recognizing former powers, but disabling an account alone cannot guarantee immediate handover by every person and institution.
copy.199: Responsibilities for handover, enforcement procedures, and responses to obstruction must still be specified by the system’s rules. Automation reduces the dependence of authority changes on an officeholder’s personal willingness; it must not be described as eliminating every practical obstacle.
copy.200: V. Rules Made by Everyone Can Also Be Wrong
copy.201: Public discussion may still lack information; qualification standards may require adjustment; a computer may faithfully execute a poorly designed rule. <mark class="key-point">Joint rule-making does not remove the need for scrutiny, and automatic implementation does not guarantee correct results.</mark>
copy.202: A system’s effectiveness depends not only on its stated principles, but also on whether errors can be discovered, reasons challenged, and corrections actually completed. The effects of both rules and system operation should be included in existing public verification and revision procedures. “That is how the system is configured” cannot justify refusing review.
copy.204: What if the conditions for revocation of authority are met but the officeholder refuses to give up power?
copy.205: Scenario An officeholder meets the formal conditions for revocation of authority, and the necessary observation and confirmation procedures are complete. Yet they demand that administrators keep following their instructions because their term has not ended.
copy.206: Answer Formal revocation of authority must not depend on voluntary cooperation. The system should revoke the corresponding system permissions according to the established result, preventing continued access to that office’s authorization within the system. Objections must follow established procedures; the officeholder cannot unilaterally declare the revocation invalid. Physical handover and noncompliance still require institutional handling. Electronic revocation does not mean all resistance has disappeared.
copy.207: If the system reports that qualifications are invalid, can verification be skipped?
copy.208: Scenario An import error causes the system to flag an officeholder’s qualifications as invalid. The person provides original documents indicating that the record may be wrong.
copy.209: Answer A system’s display reflects the application of rules to input data; it does not guarantee that the data are correct. Procedures must be established in advance for checking original records, correcting errors, and deciding whether permission changes should pause during a dispute. These are conditions that automation must address. It is inappropriate to assert either immediate revocation of authority in every case or automatic suspension of enforcement for every appeal.
copy.210: Is review still necessary if the people approved the rule and the computer applied it correctly?
copy.211: Scenario A qualification rule passes through public procedures and the system follows it exactly, but actual results show that it consistently excludes people capable of doing the job.
copy.212: Answer Correct program execution does not prove sound rule design. The cause—qualification criteria, data conditions, or something else—must still be investigated and reviewed through public procedures. Neither “the people approved it” nor “the computer calculated correctly” justifies refusing correction. Nor may individual powerholders bypass procedures and privately alter rules to obtain their preferred result.
copy.214: This concludes Volume I. The questionnaire lets you express your judgments on the public authorization framework and its institutional principles.
copy.216: Volume II / Autonomous Choice and Causal Responsibility
copy.219:
Think rationally, identify problems, and solve them.
Apply consistent standards; reject double standards.
No judgment should be influenced by human nature, emotion, morality, or ethics.
copy.220: Use facts to distinguish right from wrong, capacity to define autonomy, and causation to establish responsibility.
copy.221: My judgments rest on <mark class="key-point">decision-making capacity, available information, intent, foreseeable risks, and actual causation</mark>. Responsibility should depend on how a choice was formed, what consequences an action caused, and how much control the individual possessed. Emotional appeals, identity labels, and moral condemnation cannot replace specific reasoning.
copy.222: I advocate freedom matched with responsibility, clear and predictable rules, and public power that can be scrutinized and revoked. Every position, including my own, should be tested against evidence, logic, and institutional outcomes.
copy.223: The Scope of These Positions and Their Public Effect
copy.224: The following are my personal value judgments and policy ideas, <mark class="key-point">not necessary conditions of UPS</mark>. Family systems, tier arrangements, the scope of contracts, and the severity of punishments each require separate public reasoning and decisions. They do not become effective policies merely because of the proposer’s position.
copy.226: Eligibility for Autonomy, Contractual Validity, and Responsibility
copy.228: People must take responsibility for what they say. If you choose to give up your own human rights, the state will respect that decision too.
copy.230: Autonomy rests on decision-making capacity and arises together with corresponding responsibility.
copy.231: Those with decision-making capacity, sufficient information, freedom from coercion, and an understanding of foreseeable risks should, in principle, enjoy autonomous choice and bear its corresponding consequences. Where capacity is lacking, information concealed, or coercion present, the validity of the choice and scope of responsibility must be reassessed.
copy.232: Basic Capacity for Responsibility and Professional Qualifications
copy.233: A basic responsibility-capacity examination should first establish general eligibility for autonomy and responsibility, followed by specialized qualifications in areas such as finance and contracts. Age may serve as a reference, but does not alone prove comprehension or judgment. Necessary adjustments to examination formats should not alter the substantive abilities required.
copy.235: Subject to strict verification of capacity, informed consent, voluntariness, and valid procedures, I generally recognize long-term private contracts, including permanent ones that cannot be repudiated at will. The possibility of future regret alone does not strip all valid commitments of binding force.
copy.237: Individuals have ultimate authority over their own bodies. However, private contracts cannot dispose of third parties’ rights, privatize public political sovereignty, or independently waive public criminal liability. A personal commitment cannot bind others or descendants who have not consented.
copy.238: <mark class="key-point">Passing a capacity examination and demonstrating substantive voluntariness are separate matters.</mark> A contract still requires scrutiny for manipulation, deception, power imbalances, and coercion. Formal consent alone cannot replace substantive verification of the conditions under which the choice was made.
copy.240: Do passing a capacity examination and signing a document suffice to prove a contract valid?
copy.241: Scenario A person qualified to enter contracts signs a long-term agreement, but the other party conceals major risks and controls the person’s basic living resources to force acceptance.
copy.242: Answer Capacity, informed consent, and substantive voluntariness are separate conditions; an examination result or signature cannot prove them all. Concealment, manipulation, and coercion must still be investigated, as must the person’s ability to understand and autonomously accept the consequences. Binding force depends on these formation conditions. If they are defective, validity and responsibility must be reassessed.
copy.243: Does recognizing permanent private contracts also allow disposal of descendants’ rights or public power?
copy.244: Scenario Someone voluntarily accepts a long-term obligation that cannot be repudiated at will, while also promising to bind unborn descendants and transfer the powers of their public office to the other party.
copy.245: Answer Under my position, permanent private commitments may be valid after strict verification of capacity, informed consent, voluntariness, and procedure. Later regret alone does not automatically invalidate them. However, a person cannot dispose of the rights of others or descendants who have not consented, nor privatize public powers entrusted by the people. Private agreements likewise cannot independently waive public criminal liability.
copy.247: Responsibility for Trust, Evidentiary Standards, and Voluntary Guarantees
copy.249: All online speech should have two modes. The new mode means you are willing to stake your life on your words, emphasizing to the world that you are neither speaking out of emotion nor deliberately smearing someone.
copy.250: Trust underpins contracts, transactions, testimony, and cooperation. Responsibility assessments should distinguish mistakes after reasonable verification, unreliable sources, reckless dissemination, deliberate distortion, and knowingly false deception that exploits others’ trust. Statements should not receive identical treatment merely because they turned out to be wrong.
copy.252: <mark class="key-point">A voluntary guarantee increases the responsibility borne by its giver.</mark> It does not increase a statement’s truth or evidentiary weight, nor alter the burden of proof. Even when someone stakes their life on a claim, the case must still be decided on independent evidence.
copy.254: Those who use information reasonably considered credible at the time and fulfill reasonable verification duties do not automatically commit deliberate deception when their source is later disproved. Their knowledge, verification efforts, and subjective intent must be examined.
copy.255: Insufficient Evidence and Findings of Fact
copy.256: If the standard for conviction is not met, punishment cannot lawfully follow. But failure to prove a proposition does not establish its opposite. Judicial disposition and judgments about objective facts must each explain their evidentiary limits.
copy.257: Conditions and Criminal Liability for the Highest-Responsibility Guarantee
copy.258: For those with the required capacity who knowingly and voluntarily choose the highest-responsibility guarantee, yet still knowingly deceive and exploit others’ trust, I support extremely severe criminal penalties, <mark class="key-point">including the death penalty</mark>. This position is confined to intentional conduct meeting these conditions, not every incorrect statement.
copy.259: A guarantee cannot replace verification or bypass findings about intent, causation, and the conditions establishing responsibility. Irreversible punishments require stronger evidence, independent verification, and safeguards for review. Specific standards must be established through formal procedures.
copy.261: Does staking one’s life on a claim make it more credible than ordinary evidence?
copy.262: Scenario A witness offers the highest-responsibility guarantee that someone was at the scene, but footage, time records, and other testimony conflict.
copy.263: Answer A guarantee increases the responsibility its giver may bear, not the statement’s evidentiary weight. It does not require the accused to prove innocence. Each source must be checked independently. Even a severe guarantee cannot bypass findings of fact, knowledge, and intent. The proposed penalties under the highest-responsibility guarantee apply only to deliberate deception meeting this chapter’s strict conditions.
copy.264: If cited information is later disproved, does that make the speaker deliberately deceptive?
copy.265: Scenario A checks an original report considered credible at the time before citing its conclusion. B knows the report has been withdrawn but removes the correction and uses the original conclusion to win others’ trust.
copy.266: Answer The fact that both statements are incorrect does not establish equal responsibility. Whether A fulfilled reasonable verification duties and whether B knowingly concealed information must be investigated separately. Reckless dissemination should also be distinguished from knowing fabrication. Responsibility rests on available information, verification efforts, intent, and causation; hindsight cannot replace the entire assessment.
copy.267: Does insufficient evidence to convict mean the accuser necessarily lied?
copy.268: Scenario Missing footage and uncorroborated testimony leave an allegation below the standard for conviction. Someone therefore demands immediate punishment of the accuser.
copy.269: Answer Failure to prove the alleged conduct does not prove deliberate fabrication by the accuser. Liability for false accusation or deception requires separate proof of falsity, knowledge, intent, and other relevant conditions. A judicial decision not to punish reflects evidence and applicable standards; it cannot be expanded into a definitive finding about every related fact.
copy.271: Minimum Provision, Nonhereditary Tiers, and Governing Responsibility
copy.273: Welfare should guarantee a minimum standard of subsistence for everyone, giving each person enough breathing room and time to think rather than being forced to act under pressure.
copy.274: Every country has a class system. Instead of pretending otherwise, we should acknowledge it and establish transparent rules, giving everyone the same starting point and clear paths of advancement open to all.
copy.276: Keep society functioning through responsibility; drive its progress through passion.
copy.277: Minimum subsistence provision should allow people to meet basic living needs after unemployment, leaving a family, or rejecting dependency. Its purpose is to protect real choice and the ability to exit, reducing economic control and coercion. Resources beyond the minimum are allocated by capacity, contribution, and institutional rules.
copy.278: Minimum Subsistence Provision and the Ability to Exit
copy.279: Individuals may refuse to receive or use provision, but cannot unilaterally and permanently cancel the basic provision reserved for them. copy.282: The greater the governing authority, the stricter the responsibility, scrutiny, and restrictions on private interests.
copy.283: Management tiers must undergo eligibility reviews and continuing assessments, bearing greater governing responsibility. copy.484: Tier Changes, Departure from Office, and Restoration
copy.485: Support needs and grounds for restrictions are reviewed regularly. When capacity improves, restrictions expire, or responsibility is fulfilled, the corresponding tier is restored according to still-valid qualifications.
copy.486: Principles for Provision and Resource Allocation
copy.487: Arrangements to stop reserving provision should prioritize a revocable model, specifying application, acceptance, cessation, and restoration conditions. Acceptance by the welfare institution requires confirmation by both sides. Refusing receipt once does not constitute permanent relinquishment.
copy.488: During a resource crisis, priority should be given to reducing nonessential consumption, adjusting allocations, and necessary labor to maintain basic provision and society’s continued operation. Resource allocation requires reasons open to public scrutiny. Tier rank must not be equated directly with the value of a life.
copy.489: Advancement, assessments, and resource allowances must be reviewed under explicit rules. Gifts or private transfers of benefits must not evade eligibility restrictions. Specific scores and allowances are implementation rules and should be established through verifiable conditions and public procedures.
copy.491: If someone previously refused minimum provision, do they lose the right to seek help later?
copy.492: Scenario Someone with sufficient income refuses provision, then reapplies after losing their job. Another person previously agreed with the welfare institution to suspend the reservation of an allocation.
copy.493: Answer Refusal on one occasion is not permanent relinquishment. Stopping reservations requires the individual’s application and a bilateral arrangement with the welfare institution. Conditions for cessation, withdrawal of the arrangement, and restoration should be clear in advance, prioritizing a revocable model. The two situations must follow their respective arrangements; refusing receipt, stopping reservations, and permanent loss of rights must not be treated as identical.
copy.494: Does a tier system mean higher-tier people and their descendants enjoy permanent advantages?
copy.495: Scenario A manager previously qualified through ability and contribution but no longer meets assessment requirements. Someone close to them wants to inherit the same status and resource allowance.
copy.496: Answer Tier eligibility requires public conditions for advancement, demotion, and restoration. It cannot be retained forever merely because it was once obtained, and cannot transfer automatically through bloodline or private relationships. Ordinary eligibility provides a common starting point, with resources and powers allocated under valid rules. Tier rank also cannot be equated directly with the value of a life.
copy.497: Can an official claim that accepting private gifts has nothing to do with public responsibility?
copy.498: Scenario Rather than increasing an official’s salary directly, a supplier provides resources beyond institutional limits through holiday gifts or private transfers of benefits.
copy.499: Answer In my management-tier proposal, officials may not use gifts or extra benefits to bypass salary, asset, and resource limits. Review should examine actual benefits and transfer relationships, not merely labels. Greater governing authority demands stricter assessment and limits on interests. Personal relationships cannot make public powers a tool for exchanging benefits.
copy.500: Can Supreme Governance retain its highest investigative authority after a case ends?
copy.501: Scenario A national leader receives public authorization to investigate a specific corruption case. After the case ends, the leader still demands the same powers to investigate other matters.
copy.502: Answer Supreme Governance is a temporary status for a specified case. When the case ends, the person returns to National Leadership, and project investigative powers and assigned resources terminate. Both tiers having a decision weight of 10.0× does not permit permanent retention or unilateral expansion of investigative authority. Other cases require separate valid authorization.
copy.503: Does qualifying for Merit Provision mean retirement or the highest decision weight?
copy.504: Scenario One person qualifies through long-term accumulation near retirement age. Another earns credits for outstanding contributions and qualifies early while continuing to work.
copy.505: Answer Qualifying for Merit Provision and retiring are separate matters. Credits for outstanding contributions or exceptional performance may permit early qualification while the person continues working. This tier offers the highest overall benefits while maintaining an ordinary decision multiplier of 0.5×; benefits do not translate directly into voting power. Any separate governing office still requires reassessment under that office’s conditions and oversight rules.
copy.507: The Legal Status of Blood Relations, Public Childcare, and Independent Judgment
copy.509: Most countries require no qualification examination for parents, leaving no shortage of unfit parents. Children should be raised collectively by the state, with equalized educational resources and emotional or moral blackmail eliminated at its root.
copy.510: In my ideal system, <mark class="key-point">biological parent–child relationships remain permanently confidential</mark>. Blood relations do not automatically confer parental rights, support obligations, inheritance privileges, or hereditary benefits. Redesigning the legal family structure would prevent institutional status and access to resources from being determined by birth relationships that individuals cannot choose.
copy.512: Public institutions should undertake childcare, assigning qualified professionals by competence and establishing continuing oversight and accountability. Educational and care quality should be institutionally protected, reducing the decisive influence of family wealth, connections, and differences in upbringing on a person’s starting point in life.
copy.514: Education should cultivate verification, reasoning, questioning, and correction. Textbooks, teachers, and governments must offer reasons and accept scrutiny. Authority must not demand unquestioning obedience.
copy.516: Reject unequal beginnings at birth; prohibit unfit parenthood.
copy.517: Distinguishing Voluntary Relationships from the Legal Effects of Blood Relations
copy.518: The absence of automatic legal benefits from blood relations does not prevent people from voluntarily forming emotional bonds, companionship, and intimate relationships. Rights and duties within relationships should rest on valid consent, actual conduct, and applicable rules.
copy.519: Permanent confidentiality of biological parent–child relationships must remain consistent with inheritance, support, and succession arrangements. A system cannot prevent public access to bloodline identities while simultaneously presuming known parent–child relationships as a basis for allocating rights.
copy.520: Population Planning and Optimal Living Space
copy.521: My population position starts from sustainable living conditions, rather than treating a larger population or higher birth rate as the sole objective. Habitable land, resource supply, labor demand, population losses, and care and educational capacity should inform separate assessments of the maximum supportable population and a more suitable size, ensuring sufficient living space and public resources for everyone.
copy.522: When population is below a suitable level, reproduction would be permitted under qualification rules and encouraged. Near carrying capacity, reproductive conditions and scale would be adjusted through public assessment. This proposal addresses both low birth rates and excessive population growth. A single birth-rate indicator cannot replace judgments about long-term resources, age structure, and quality of life. Specific thresholds and restrictions require further argument; population projections do not themselves authorize arbitrary intervention in individual bodies.
copy.523: Professional Gestational Mothers and Public Child-Rearing
copy.524: I support recognizing gestation and childbirth services as a profession undertaken voluntarily, without compulsory employment to fill a shortfall in births. Professional gestational mothers undertake reproductive and gestational roles. <mark class="key-point">Childbearing, parental rights, and qualifications for actual care are assessed separately.</mark> Giving birth does not automatically confer parental rights or impose a personal duty to support the child.
copy.525: Public institutions bear newborn care and education costs, providing care by qualified professionals through arrangements involving multiple caregivers and children, with caregiver rotation. Biological parents’ and children’s identities follow the confidentiality principle. Biological parents cannot use blood relations to gain priority in caring for their own children. Care quality and educational content remain subject to public oversight.
copy.526: Professional qualifications, remuneration, health protection, risk disclosure, service termination, and the limits of contractual responsibility require separate rules. Review must follow this volume’s principles of capacity, informed consent, and substantive voluntariness. Neither a signature nor population needs constitute complete proof of consent.
copy.528: Does removing legal privileges based on blood relations also reject private affection and companionship?
copy.529: Scenario A child in public care forms a deep bond with a long-term caregiver. Both wish to remain in contact under the applicable rules.
copy.530: Answer Removing parental rights, support obligations, inheritance, or hereditary benefits arising automatically from blood relations does not prohibit voluntarily formed emotional relationships. Rights and duties should follow valid consent, actual conduct, and applicable rules; care qualifications and responsibilities require professional oversight. Under permanent confidentiality of biological parent–child relationships, known bloodline identity cannot remain a default basis for resource allocation.
copy.531: Does public childcare and education mean the government can require uniform thought?
copy.532: Scenario A student identifies inadequate sources in a textbook and presents a well-supported counterexample to a government claim. The teacher demands acceptance solely because the textbook is official.
copy.533: Answer Under my educational position, textbooks, teachers, and governments must all give reasons and accept scrutiny. Education should cultivate verification, reasoning, questioning, and correction; authority cannot replace evidence. Public care entails responsibility for care quality and accountability; it does not confer unquestionable authority in matters of thought.
copy.534: Can increasing the number of professional gestational mothers solve population problems by itself?
copy.535: Scenario One area has few births, but also inadequate public childcare, staff training, and suitable living space. Another is already approaching its resource carrying capacity.
copy.536: Answer Professional gestational motherhood is one arrangement within the population proposal, not a substitute for public child-rearing and resource planning. The first area must also consider care, education, and long-term living conditions. The second should not expand reproduction solely to increase births. Population policy should adapt to continually updated conditions, rather than presuming that more people is always better.
copy.538: Clear Rules, Subjective Intent, and Criminal Responsibility
copy.540: Minors, the elderly, people with mental illness, those who are drunk or using drugs, and others should have no special privileges. Those who deserve to die must still die.
copy.541: Honesty is a duty, not a virtue. Telling the truth is not difficult. Lying is an extreme evil that destroys human trust; its harmful effects exceed those of murder and arson.
copy.542: Behavioral requirements maintained through public coercive power should clearly specify prohibited conditions, who bears responsibility, and legal consequences, so people can understand the cost of their actions in advance. Public punishment must follow predictable rules and must not be increased solely through emotional condemnation or moral pressure formed afterward.
copy.544: When someone does not know the rule or misunderstands the situation, they should first be informed and given an opportunity to correct their conduct. Only deliberate violations after understanding enter the corresponding assessment of intentional responsibility. Subjective malice and actual harm must be examined separately; neither substitutes for the other.
copy.546: A person who commits a crime after voluntarily drinking or using drugs is not automatically excused because judgment later deteriorates. Coercion or unknowingly being drugged requires assessment under different conditions of causation and control. Identities such as age or sex cannot alone justify unexplained differences in responsibility.
copy.548: Offenses, sentence lengths, compulsory obligations, and losses to be borne are established in advance by public law. Forgiveness by victims or related persons may improve accommodation, food, or conditions of sentence execution only within legally preset limits. Compensation may be a condition of forgiveness, but cannot purchase exemption from core criminal liability.
copy.550: For purely malicious acts involving continued deliberate violation of known rules after clear notice, I support extremely severe penalties, including <mark class="key-point">making deliberate queue-jumping potentially punishable by death</mark>. In this view of responsibility, clear malice may be more blameworthy than harm from an unintentional accident. Knowledge and intent must be rigorously established.
copy.551: This is my personal position on punishment, not a necessary part of UPS. The more irreversible a punishment, the stronger the required evidence, independent verification, and review should be. Irreversible measures must not be carried out where substantive doubt remains. Specific evidentiary rules require separate formal procedures.
copy.552: Traffic Risks and Responsibility for Life and Property
copy.553: My traffic-responsibility proposal uses the advance risk priority “unlicensed driving > drug-impaired driving > drunk driving > running a red light > speeding.” It aims to clarify risk and responsibility boundaries. It is an institutional proposal, not a statement of current accident-liability rules.
copy.554: Deliberately driving into another person should first be treated as an intentional attack, outside ordinary accident comparisons. I propose that those without helmets bear their own risk to life: if they die in an accident, the other party does not owe compensation for loss of life, while property losses such as damage to the motorcycle remain subject to responsibility.
copy.555: For example, under this proposal, in an ordinary accident a speeding driver who kills an unlicensed driver would not owe compensation; the same applies to an ordinary driver who kills a drunk driver. Those unwilling to bear the consequences themselves in an accident should avoid the listed behaviors.
copy.556: The Effect of Rules and Limits on Law-Enforcement Questioning
copy.557: New rules may raise qualification or conduct requirements, but cannot retroactively criminalize previously lawful acts. Higher qualification standards must be addressed separately from the validity of existing qualifications, future application, and adjustment procedures.
copy.558: I advocate a duty to answer lawful and reasonable law-enforcement questions honestly. Manifestly unreasonable questions or those exceeding legitimate scope may be refused. Silence itself does not prove a specific crime; judgment must still rest on evidence.
copy.560: Should ignorance of queueing rules and knowing violation receive the same punishment?
copy.561: Scenario A does not notice where the queue is and immediately goes to the back when informed. B understands the rule, has been clearly informed, and still keeps deliberately cutting in.
copy.562: Answer Under my position on punishment, knowledge, intent, and actual conduct must first be distinguished. Misunderstanding a situation cannot simply be treated as deliberate malice. For the latter conduct, I support extremely severe penalties potentially including death. However, irreversible measures require rigorous findings of responsibility, stronger evidence, independent verification, and review safeguards. This is a personal position, not current law or a requirement of UPS.
copy.563: Is responsibility the same for losing judgment after drinking and after being drugged?
copy.564: Scenario A knows the risks but drinks voluntarily and later harms someone. B is drugged without knowing it, affecting control over subsequent actions.
copy.565: Answer Reduced capacity at the time cannot alone justify either excusing both or assigning equal responsibility. Trace the cause of the impairment and examine knowledge, voluntariness, foreseeable risks, and causation between conduct and harm. Voluntarily impairing one’s judgment does not automatically sever responsibility; unknowingly being drugged requires assessment under different control conditions.
copy.566: Can a victim’s acceptance of compensation and forgiveness remove criminal liability?
copy.567: Scenario An offender offers substantial compensation. The victim is willing to forgive and asks for the established prison term to be waived.
copy.568: Answer Under my position, compensation may be a condition of forgiveness, but cannot purchase exemption from the offense, sentence, compulsory obligations, or losses to be borne. Forgiveness may improve accommodation, food, or sentence-execution conditions only within limits set by law in advance. The core of public punishment cannot be replaced by the parties’ wealth or private agreements.
copy.569: Does a passenger’s own driving license make them responsible for a driver’s unlicensed driving?
copy.570: Scenario A knows the driver is unqualified but still chooses to entrust their safety to that person. B performs reasonable checks but is deceived by a forged qualification document.
copy.571: Answer Whether passengers hold licenses themselves does not directly determine responsibility. Examine their knowledge of the driver’s qualifications and risks, the reasonableness of their reliance, and causation between choice and consequences. Knowingly accepting an unqualified driver’s risk differs from reasonable reliance induced by deception. The driver’s own responsibility must still be assessed independently.
copy.572: Can the proposed assumption of life risk by helmetless riders also excuse someone who deliberately hits them?
copy.573: Scenario A helmetless rider dies in an ordinary accident. In another case, someone deliberately drives into an equally helmetless rider.
copy.574: Answer Under my traffic proposal, the first rider bears the risk to life, so the other party does not owe compensation for loss of life; property losses such as motorcycle damage still follow responsibility. The second case must first be assessed as an intentional attack. Ordinary accident risk rankings or helmet conditions cannot excuse deliberate harm. These are personal institutional proposals, not current accident-handling rules.
copy.575: Can higher qualification standards turn previously lawful acts into crimes?
copy.576: Scenario An operation was permitted under an old qualification. New rules raise capacity requirements, and the authority seeks to hold someone criminally responsible for operations conducted before those rules took effect.
copy.577: Answer New requirements may govern future conduct, but raising the standard alone cannot retroactively criminalize previously lawful actions. Whether existing qualifications remain valid, when new standards apply, and how adjustments occur require separate, clear procedures. A change in qualification must not be equated with prior intentional illegality.
copy.578: Does refusing to answer law-enforcement questions suffice to prove guilt?
copy.579: Scenario An officer asks about conduct related to a case, along with private questions clearly exceeding legitimate scope. The person refuses to answer the latter.
copy.580: Answer I advocate honest answers to lawful and reasonable questions, while permitting refusal of manifestly unreasonable or excessive questions. Whether a duty to answer exists and whether a particular crime occurred are different issues. Silence alone cannot prove a specific crime. Verifiable conduct and evidence are still required.
copy.582: Trust is the foundation of society; honesty is a human duty.
copy.584: Private Valuation, Liability for Harm, and Corporate Governance
copy.586: The fact that something such as affection cannot be quantified does not mean others must pay unlimited compensation.
copy.587: Businesses may grow and arrange their own succession. But when they create substantial public impact, they should face corresponding oversight.
copy.588: I believe risk, trust, and affection can, in principle, all be approached quantitatively. The amount one is willing to lend, risks one will bear, and losses one will accept can help explain private valuation. However, <mark class="key-point">subjective valuation cannot directly impose unlimited compensation duties on others</mark>.
copy.590: The loss of unique data or a keepsake may be irreparable, and scarcity may affect value. Preservation, remedies, and compensation still depend on specific conditions. Irreversibility itself does not mean infinite value.
copy.592: I do not prescribe a fixed ceiling on business size, but businesses with public impact should face corresponding oversight. Control and succession require lawful designation, competence, or another valid institutional basis. They do not arise automatically from blood relations and cannot become irrevocable public power.
copy.594:
Imagine different individuals becoming ill:
If it were a stranger, how much would you pay for them?
If it were a particular friend, how much would you pay?
If it were a family member, how much would you pay?
If it were your partner, how much would you pay?
If it were your pet, how much would you pay?
If it were you, how much would you pay for yourself?
This is one way to quantify affection. Similar comparisons can be made in other areas.
copy.596: Money is not something vulgar; it is a quantification of value.
copy.598: Personal importance may inform damage assessment, but demanding compensation from others still requires verifiable grounds for causation, rights, and valuation. Subjective feelings and publicly enforceable responsibility must be justified separately.
copy.600: I advocate limits on accumulated personal assets, with different allowances by tier eligibility, to constrain long-term concentration of resources among a few. Cash, deposits, stocks, funds, and other financial assets should all count toward total personal assets under consistent valuation rules. Changing the form of ownership cannot exclude them from accounting.
copy.601: <mark class="key-point">Asset limits constrain accumulation; spending limits constrain personal use within a period.</mark> Assets are assessed at fixed intervals, provisionally illustrated as annual. Excess must be returned to the system within a specified deadline, with any unhandled balance dealt with under public rules. Spending is capped separately, so heavy spending just before assessment cannot also defeat consumption limits. Actual periods, valuation methods, return mechanisms, and exceptions remain to be specified.
copy.602: Personal assets and business assets genuinely used for production and operations should be calculated separately. Businesses may continue growing, but company ownership cannot conceal personal holdings or private consumption. The tier diagram’s “low, medium, high” labels indicate relative allocations, not established monetary amounts. Minimum subsistence and necessary care must also be stated separately from personal allowances.
copy.604: Does a unique, irreplaceable keepsake have unlimited compensation value?
copy.605: Scenario A custodian loses a photograph with no backup. To its owner it is irreplaceable, perhaps more important than expensive possessions.
copy.606: Answer I recognize that affection, scarcity, and irreversible loss may enter discussions of value, but uniqueness does not automatically create unlimited liability. Custodial responsibility, causation, possible remedies, and valuation grounds still require examination. Being immensely important to its owner and determining how much another person must legally bear are separate questions.
copy.607: Does having no business-size limit allow private wealth to dominate public power?
copy.608: Scenario A large company lawfully appoints a competent employee as successor, then claims its economic influence entitles it to public decision-making power that the people cannot revoke.
copy.609: Answer Corporate control may follow lawful designation, competence, or another valid institutional basis; it does not arise automatically from blood relations. However, succession in a private business cannot extend to inheritance of public sovereignty. Rejecting a fixed business-size ceiling does not preclude regulation based on public impact, much less permit wealth to become irrevocable public power.
copy.610: Can placing stocks or private expenses under a company’s name bypass personal limits?
copy.611: Scenario Someone labels personal investments and leisure spending as corporate use, arguing that separately calculated business assets need not appear in personal accounting.
copy.612: Answer Assessment should examine actual use and who benefits, not merely the registered name. Personal stocks, funds, and other financial assets count toward the personal total; assets genuinely used in business production and operations are counted separately. Company names cannot shield personal benefits or consumption from limits. Specific recognition and valuation procedures must be established publicly.
copy.614: This questionnaire uses social issues to compare my blunt and more formally worded answers, helping you see where your views overlap with mine and where they differ. There are no standard answers and no grading of right or wrong. It is a comparison of positions, not a knowledge test.
copy.617: The Scope, Conditions, and Practical Principles of These Positions
copy.619: This text has two levels: how public power is authorized and revoked, and the specific arrangements I personally favor. You can judge them separately without accepting or rejecting the whole package.
copy.620: These principles also do not mean every threshold, deadline, and implementation method has been settled. To become public rules, conditions, evidence, and safeguards must be clarified, followed by the appropriate discussion, review, and decisions.
copy.622: Popular sovereignty, continuing authorization, and effective revocation of authority form the core of UPS. Asset limits, population and family policies, tiers, punishment, and extreme contracts are personal positions. Open information, corresponding responsibility, and revisability run through both the public system and personal thought.
copy.624: Support thresholds, observation periods, qualification scores, and resource allowances must be established according to applicable conditions and public procedures. <mark class="key-point">A statement of principle is not a complete set of implementation rules.</mark> Specific regulations cannot rest solely on examples or personal preferences.
copy.625: Evidence Requirements and Limits of Application
copy.626: Substantive voluntariness, irreversible punishment, and institutional transitions all involve highly significant rights and risks. Their application requires clear disclosure of conditions, evidence, and safeguards. Abstract promises cannot replace specific scrutiny.
copy.628: This text presents a public authorization framework and my personal positions. Each claim should be examined separately for factual grounds, consistent reasoning, boundaries of rights, and practical effects. Support for or dislike of its proposer does not remove the need for argument.
copy.629: Any proposal seeking public coercive force must pass the relevant discussion, review, and decision-making procedures. <mark class="key-point">A personal position does not directly constitute law.</mark> A system’s name cannot guarantee correct decisions either; its legitimacy must remain under scrutiny through authorization, implementation, and responsibility.
copy.630: Every problem has a best answer, and there is always room to do better.
